questions.question: Why is 'labeling' (assigning letters/numbers to vertices) recommended before counting complex figures?
options: It lets you refer to and track specific points and combinations precisely and unambiguously, avoiding visual confusion
It has no real benefit
It is only useful for triangles, not other shapes
It replaces the need for any counting method
questions.rationale: Labeling vertices lets you precisely and unambiguously refer to specific points and combinations, which avoids the confusion that comes with purely visual tracking.

questions.question: What does the 'vertex-path method' involve?
options: Ignoring vertices entirely
Only tracing the outer boundary
Systematically tracing paths between labeled vertices to identify every valid closed figure
Randomly connecting vertices
questions.rationale: This method systematically traces paths between labeled vertices, using that tracing to identify every valid closed figure in the diagram.

questions.question: What is 'candidate validation' in a figure-counting algorithm?
options: Skipping verification to save time
Checking that a proposed combination of segments actually forms a genuinely closed, valid figure before counting it
Only validating the largest figure
Validating the figure's color scheme
questions.rationale: Candidate validation confirms that a proposed combination of segments truly forms a closed, valid figure before it's added to the count — catching false positives.

questions.question: What is 'composite figure detection'?
options: Detecting only the smallest figures
Removing composite figures from the count entirely
Detecting figures made of a single color
Identifying larger figures formed by combining two or more adjacent basic figures
questions.rationale: Composite figure detection identifies larger figures built by combining two or more adjacent basic figures, which is a distinct step from counting the basic figures themselves.

questions.question: What is the main purpose of a formal 'figure-counting algorithm'?
options: To provide a repeatable, systematic sequence of steps that reliably finds every valid figure without missing or double-counting any
To make the process more confusing
To only work on grid-based figures
To replace the need for any verification
questions.rationale: A formal algorithm provides a repeatable, systematic sequence of steps designed to reliably find every valid figure while avoiding both missed and double-counted figures.

questions.question: What is one 'common mistake' this lesson likely warns about in figure counting?
options: Using too many labels
Counting too systematically
Missing hidden or overlapping figures formed by combinations of basic shapes, not just the most visually obvious ones
Using formulas at all
questions.rationale: A very common mistake is missing hidden or overlapping composite figures, focusing only on the most visually obvious basic shapes.

questions.question: What does a 'mistake prevention chart' help with?
options: Drawing the figure more neatly
Summarizing the most common counting errors (missing figures, double-counting, boundary traps) as a quick checklist to review against
Choosing which color to use
Replacing the figure-counting algorithm entirely
questions.rationale: This chart consolidates the most common errors into a quick-reference checklist, letting you review your work against known pitfalls before finalizing an answer.

questions.question: When is it appropriate to use a direct formula (like the squares-in-a-grid formula) rather than manual counting?
options: Never — manual counting is always required
Only for triangles, never for squares or rectangles
Only when the figure has no lines at all
When the figure follows a regular, well-defined structure that a known formula directly applies to
questions.rationale: Direct formulas apply reliably when a figure has a regular, well-defined structure (like a uniform grid) that matches the formula's underlying assumptions.

questions.question: What is the difference between a 'regular' and an 'irregular' figure in this context?
options: There is no meaningful difference
A regular figure follows a predictable, uniform structure (like a grid) that formulas can be applied to directly; an irregular figure doesn't, and usually requires manual systematic counting instead
Irregular figures are always larger
Regular figures never contain triangles
questions.rationale: Regular figures have a predictable, uniform structure that known formulas can be applied to directly, while irregular figures require the manual, systematic counting approach instead.

questions.question: What is the purpose of a 'formula selection tree'?
options: To randomly pick a formula
To help decide which specific counting formula or method applies, based on the type and structure of the figure given
To eliminate the need for any formulas
To only apply to circle-based problems
questions.rationale: A formula selection tree guides you toward the correct formula or method to apply, based on identifying the type and structure of the specific figure given.
